newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: San Miguel core business seen threatened.
newsitem.headline: San Miguel core business seen threatened.

text.p: In the Philippines, the health of the economy is not always measured by growth figures or export volumes.
Some use the sales of beer as a barometer, and in particular, the performance of San Miguel Corp, the country's largest brewer and a household name across the archipelago.
Started more than a century ago in the district of San Miguel in the old walled city of Manila, the beer company sprouted simply because one product led to another.
In the 1920s, Andres Soriano y Roxas, grandfather of the current chairman Andres Soriano y Roxas III, installed a refrigeration unit for the beers.

Making further use of the cooling unit, it ventured into ice cream. Since the malt by-product from brewing beer made good cattle-feed, it went into feeds, and to make sure the feed was sold, San Miguel got into the poultry business.
The product mix was a success for decades, but in the past five years a higher tax burden and increasing competition have been affecting San Miguel's core business, beer.
"The threat is real now," San Miguel chief financial officer Delfin Gonzalez said.
"You see lots of products from overseas coming in... very good quality and in many cases, priced quite competitively."
San Miguel, a blue-chip share on the Philippine Stock Exchange, said this week that 1996 net profits, inclusive of a one-time gain, grew just four percent to 5.84 billion pesos (US$222 million).
But one day after the results were announced, investors were still buying the stock, even though it is relatively expensive at 40 times its earnings.
"I think the growth is going to be there and that is justifying the valuation of San Miguel in the minds of investors," Gonzalez said.
Stock brokerage Asia Equity Philippines disagrees.
"I just don't get it," research head Matthew Sutherland said.
He said "rising costs and declining purchasing power" in the Philippines over the past seven years had cast doubt on the beer sector's potential for growth.
San Miguel believes that although growth in domestic beer sales has declined in the past few years, the country's improving economic situation will help the company's bottom line.
The Philippines annually consumes about 180 million cases of beer, each containing 24 bottles of 320 millilitres.
The demand has fallen from 200 million cases in the 1980s, and with San Miguel having over 80 percent of the market, it has felt the slowdown the most.
To counter the situation, San Miguel ventured into overseas beer markets, particularly in China.
The main brake on the Filipino propensity for drinking beer has been steep taxes. Sixty percent of San Miguel's price goes towards taxes.
Another factor threatening to make the local beer business go flat is the growing prosperity that has made many Filipinos health-conscious.

"Reflecting the shifting market dynamics, juices and the so-called 'New Age' beverages -- health drinks, sports drinks, energy tonics, and various waters -- posted substantially faster growth rates than traditional beverages -- soft drinks, beer and hard liquor," San Miguel's 1995 annual report said.
A small segment of San Miguel's business, mineral water, has been the company's fastest-growing unit in the past three years, surging by 40 to 50 percent annually.
San Miguel's 1995 annual report said the future belonged to taking "a fresh look at strategy and charting new directions."
